title: Thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive models for elastoplasticity via eigen-representations
authors: Harikrishnan Vijayakumaran, Shunyu Yin, Martin Abendroth, Miguel A. Bessa, Karl A. Kalina
abstract: Neural network material models can represent yield surfaces and hardening laws with far more flexibility than classical closed-form plasticity formulations, but training such a model end-to-end through an implicit return map introduces non-trivial challenges. This work presents a thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive model for rate-independent, isotropic elastoplasticity that jointly learns a flexible yield function together with its evolution laws. For non-associative flow, the yield function extends the convex flow potential by a jointly trained additive term, which renders the model thermodynamically consistent by construction. Isotropy and convexity are enforced simultaneously across all learnable components through a permutation-invariant, spectral (eigenvalue-based) representation. Training proceeds through a backward-Euler return map, with gradients propagated by the implicit function theorem together with an eigenvalue-degeneracy-aware scheme for safe differentiation. The robustness and generality of the approach are demonstrated by reproducing known constitutive models, including non-associative flow, learning material behavior from stress--strain data extracted from a full-field finite element simulation, and capturing unknown non-associative behavior from homogenized representative volume elements of a foam. Finally, the proposed neural plasticity model is evaluated within finite element simulations to solve boundary-value-problem under plane stress.

infographic.key_insight: Eigenvalue-based neural constitutive models jointly learn flexible yield functions and evolution laws while enforcing isotropy, convexity, and thermodynamic consistency by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables learned rate-independent elastoplastic material behavior, including non-associative flow, to be used in finite element boundary-value simulations.
method: Use permutation-invariant spectral representations to enforce isotropy and convexity.
Construct non-associative yield functions by adding a jointly learned term to a convex flow potential.
Train through a backward-Euler return map using implicit gradients and eigenvalue-degeneracy-aware differentiation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation includes reproducing known constitutive models, learning from full-field finite element stress–strain data and homogenized foam responses, and solving plane-stress boundary-value problems.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation requires careful implicit-solver differentiation near repeated eigenvalues; the stated scope is rate-independent, isotropic elastoplasticity.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive models for elastoplasticity via eigen-representations

title: Dynamic Prandtl-Reuss Thermoplasticity with Degenerating Yield Constraints
abstract: We study a three-dimensional dynamic thermoplastic system with a temperature-dependent convex yield set whose deviatoric section may collapse completely at a finite temperature. The underlying constitutive model is rate-independent Prandtl-Reuss perfect plasticity, without Kelvin-Voigt viscosity, hardening, or a safe-load condition. We construct global approximation-generated relaxed entropy-energy states by a one-parameter Temam-Norton-Hoff-Galerkin scheme with an undiscretized heat equation and untruncated plastic heat production. The logarithmic temperature is strongly compact in $L^2(0,T;L^q(Ω))$ for every $q<6$ and in $L^p((0,T)\timesΩ)$ for every $p<8/3$. An entropy-weighted work estimate yields convergence of the overstress at rate $O(\sqrt{\log n/n})$ in every fixed finite Lebesgue space and identifies stress admissibility. The constitutive limit comprises a distributional plastic balance, finite support-weighted measures, and compact-fibre lifts carrying exact normality and maximum plastic work. A locally finite lift on the positive-radius fibres unifies the level-restricted limits at every continuity level. At the macroscopic level, however, the available compactness does not identify a canonical stress-plastic-flow pairing. Moreover, an explicit smooth state satisfying the intrinsic relaxed balance conditions shows that these conditions do not imply macroscopic Prandtl-Reuss normality. In the fully collapsed regime, an energy-entropy rigidity argument determines the evolution and yields approximation-generated examples in which the plastic flow need not be a finite measure or the displacement need not retain its full boundary trace. Thermal concentration and plastic entropy production remain explicit throughout.

infographic.key_insight: Global relaxed entropy-energy states can be constructed for dynamic thermoplasticity even when the temperature-dependent yield set collapses, but macroscopic Prandtl-Reuss normality is not guaranteed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The analysis clarifies constitutive limits for thermomechanical models whose plastic strength can vanish at finite temperature, without viscosity or hardening regularization.
method: One-parameter Temam-Norton-Hoff-Galerkin approximation with an undiscretized heat equation.
Entropy-weighted estimates establish logarithmic-temperature compactness and stress admissibility.
Measure-valued limits and compact-fibre lifts encode exact normality and maximum plastic work.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical results include an O(sqrt(log n/n)) overstress convergence rate in every fixed finite Lebesgue space and an explicit smooth counterexample to macroscopic normality; the abstract reports no numerical validation.
infographic.watch_item: Available compactness does not identify a canonical macroscopic stress-plastic-flow pairing, and fully collapsed regimes may lose finite-measure plastic flow or the full displacement boundary trace.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamic Prandtl-Reuss Thermoplasticity with Degenerating Yield Constraints

title: A scaling law for numerical computation of fracture stress intensity factors
authors: Ronghao Cui, Jan Martin Nordbotten, Ivar Stefansson, Inga Berre
abstract: Numerical simulations of fracture propagation require accurate computation of stress intensity factors (SIFs) to determine whether a pre-existing fracture will propagate. Even though displacement solutions from well-established numerical methods generally converge with mesh refinement, the convergence behavior of SIF estimates remains less understood. In this work, we propose a scaling law to improve the performance of SIF extraction using two-point displacement correlation methods. This scaling law relates sampling distance from the fracture tip to mesh resolution. It is developed by balancing the asymptotic truncation error against the numerical discretization error. Three numerical discretization methods--standard quadratic finite elements, quadratic finite elements with quarter-point elements, and a multi-point stress approximation finite volume method--are employed to validate the proposed scaling law on fracture benchmark problems under pure-mode and mixed-mode loading. We find that the conventional nearest-tip sampling strategy fails to compute convergent SIF estimates. In contrast, the proposed scaling-based approach yields decreasing errors in the SIF estimates as the mesh is refined. Across all three discretization methods, the proposed scaling law captures the sampling locations required for convergent SIF extraction, suggesting a general numerical characteristic of near-tip SIF extraction.

infographic.key_insight: Linking displacement-sampling distance to mesh resolution enables convergent stress intensity factor estimates where conventional nearest-tip sampling fails.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More reliable stress intensity factors support accurate decisions about whether pre-existing fractures will propagate in numerical simulations.
method: Balance near-tip asymptotic truncation error against numerical discretization error.
Use the resulting scaling law to select sampling distances for two-point displacement correlation.
Test standard quadratic finite elements, quarter-point quadratic finite elements, and multi-point stress approximation finite volumes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across fracture benchmarks with pure-mode and mixed-mode loading, all three discretization methods showed decreasing SIF errors with scaling-based sampling as meshes were refined, unlike nearest-tip sampling.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify the scaling formula or its applicability beyond the tested methods and benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: A scaling law for numerical computation of fracture stress intensity factors

title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity
authors: Lianghao Cao, George Stepaniants, Andrew M. Stuart
abstract: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.

infographic.key_insight: Microstructure-dependent recurrent neural operators can approximate homogenized Kelvin–Voigt constitutive laws uniformly across time, admissible loading histories, and material fields in 2D and 3D.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These surrogates aim to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations while retaining microstructure-dependent, history-sensitive material responses.
method: Encode loading-history dependence with Markovian internal variables.
Learn microstructure-dependent constitutive responses using neural operators.
Use spectral memory-kernel approximation to bound sufficient internal-variable dimension logarithmically in inverse relative stress error and material contrast.
infographic.evidence_signal: Unit-cell-data experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity examine internal-variable dimension and sample complexity; theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.
infographic.watch_item: The approximation guarantee covers periodic Kelvin–Voigt viscoelasticity, not general nonlinear inelasticity; crystal plasticity is supported by numerical experiments.
infographic.paper_title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity

title: Numerical analysis of coupled flow, deformation and frictional contact mechanics in a fractured porous medium
authors: Marius Nevland, Kundan Kumar, Inga Berre, Jakub Wiktor Both, Eirik Keilegavlen
abstract: This paper studies the numerical approximation of a mathematical model of coupled flow and viscoelastic deformation in a fractured porous medium including fracture contact mechanics. We consider a mixed-dimensional model, where the fracture is modeled as a co-dimension one object within the porous medium. This model couples Darcy flow in the matrix and fracture, linear viscoelasticity of the matrix and frictional contact mechanics of the fracture surfaces; the contact conditions include normal compliance and a Coulomb friction law. We propose and analyze a fully discrete numerical scheme for this problem, using conformal finite elements in space and the implicit Euler method in time. Existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution is established, and stability and a priori error estimates are derived. A numerical experiment is performed in which numerical error estimates are computed and compared to the theoretical results.

infographic.key_insight: A fully discrete mixed-dimensional model couples porous flow, viscoelastic deformation and frictional fracture contact, with proven discrete well-posedness and error bounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports numerical analysis of fractured porous materials where fluid transport, deformation and fracture slip interact.
method: Couple matrix and fracture Darcy flow with linear viscoelastic matrix deformation.
Represent fractures as co-dimension-one interfaces with normal compliance and Coulomb friction.
Discretize using conformal finite elements in space and implicit Euler in time.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper establishes discrete existence, uniqueness, stability and a priori error estimates, then compares computed numerical errors with theory in one numerical experiment.
infographic.watch_item: Validation described in the abstract is limited to one numerical experiment; broad applicability to complex fracture networks is not demonstrated there.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical analysis of coupled flow, deformation and frictional contact mechanics in a fractured porous medium

title: SiC-BN composites with extreme thermal and environmental stability
authors: Abhijit Biswas, Eugenio Garcia-Granados, Saman Zare, Mozhdeh Mirakhory, JungHun Park, Shuvodeep De
abstract: Ceramic materials that maintain structural integrity and resist thermal-shock under extreme conditions are critical for many applications. Here we show that spark plasma sintered composites containing equal weight fractions of hexagonal silicon carbide (6H-SiC) and boron nitride (h-BN) exhibit exceptional stability under extreme high-temperature oxidizing conditions and unusually stable temperature-independent thermal conductivity across a broad temperature range. Under high-velocity oxygen-fuel torch exposure in air, it withstands prolonged heating and thermal-cycling at surface temperatures reaching >1500 °C, whereas pure 6H-SiC and h-BN rapidly fractures or erodes. Microstructural evaluation shows the formation of a multi-phase surface silica layer that further protects the material from oxidation. Finite-element analysis heat-flux map shows that intrinsic porosity mitigates thermal stress, while ReaxFF molecular dynamics simulations reveal thermally driven interfacial reconstruction and the formation of a Si-N/C-B-rich bonding network, enhancing the interfacial cohesion at elevated temperatures. This lightweight, easily machinable ceramic composite will be a promising structural material in extreme environment applications.

infographic.key_insight: A spark-plasma-sintered composite with equal weight fractions of 6H-SiC and h-BN maintains structural integrity under extreme oxidizing heat and exhibits nearly temperature-independent thermal conductivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This lightweight, machinable ceramic is a promising candidate for structural components exposed to severe heating and thermal cycling.
method: Spark plasma sintering of equal-weight 6H-SiC and h-BN.
Oxygen-fuel torch testing and microstructural evaluation.
Finite-element thermal analysis and ReaxFF molecular dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The composite survived prolonged torch heating and thermal cycling at surface temperatures above 1500 °C, while pure 6H-SiC and h-BN rapidly fractured or eroded.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify exposure duration, cycle count, or retained mechanical strength, limiting assessment of long-term service reliability.
infographic.paper_title: SiC-BN composites with extreme thermal and environmental stability

title: Ultrasound Elastography: Excitation Methods and Low-Cost Alternative
abstract: Ultrasound elastography (or elasticity imaging) is a method that characterizes the tissue mechanical properties with the purpose of aiding the diagnosis of certain pathologies. Many novel clinical applications use the assumption that these tissue properties are changed in the presence of pathological processes. Characterization of tissue mechanical properties is achieved by imaging the response of the tissue to an induced stress or excitation. A plethora of approaches have been used in the scientific community to induce excitation in tissue, which usually require additional tools or devices than are costly. Furthermore these are usually integrated in the imaging pipeline using additional software or hardware for control. An alternative that is simpler, faster to integrate (and low-cost) is proposed in this work, by using readily available smartphones as a source of mechanical excitation. The induced displacements are used to solve the elasticity inverse problem (IP) using a finite element method (FEM) approach. Preliminary elasticity reconstructions of a phantom that mimics tissue are similar to when using a dedicated actuator as means of inducing harmonic displacements, illustrating the feasibility of our low-cost ultrasound elasography approach.

infographic.key_insight: A readily available smartphone can provide low-cost mechanical excitation for ultrasound elastography, with preliminary tissue-phantom reconstructions similar to those obtained using a dedicated actuator.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Smartphone-based excitation could reduce equipment costs and simplify integration of tissue stiffness imaging.
method: Use a smartphone to mechanically excite a tissue-mimicking phantom.
Image the induced tissue displacements with ultrasound.
Recover elasticity by solving an inverse problem using finite element methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: Preliminary phantom experiments produced elasticity reconstructions similar to those obtained with dedicated-actuator harmonic excitation; the abstract reports no quantitative accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Clinical performance and excitation reproducibility remain unestablished by the preliminary phantom results.
infographic.paper_title: Ultrasound Elastography: Excitation Methods and Low-Cost Alternative

title: Physics-constrained differentiable causal discovery of constitutive mechanisms through boundary value problems
abstract: Data-driven constitutive model discovery is recast as causal discovery of mechanism parent sets using time-unrolled structural causal models. Hard-coding balance laws and constitutive skeletons, candidate graphs score environment--mechanism and state--state edges via weak-form equilibrium gaps evaluated from full-field displacements, avoiding the need to measure stresses or internal variables. An adaptive lasso and a NOTEARS-type constraint ensure graph acyclicity and an explicit evaluation order, treating climate-chamber protocols as interventions. Automatic differentiation yields the score's Gauss--Newton matrix as a local identifiability certificate, driving greedy D-optimal test design. In a synthetic study on a hygro-thermo-viscoelastic damaging plate (8 true edges among 13 candidates), interventional data recover the exact true graph in 7 of 10 runs (0.01px displacement noise) with zero attribution error. Conversely, observational data with a temperature--moisture correlation of $-0.998$ fail entirely because confounded scores are 250--380 times flatter. Observationally discovered models reproduce training climates (3.6% error) but mispredict hot and humid climates by up to 41.5% (16.9% average), whereas interventionally discovered models stay within 3.2%. A correlation sweep shows the certificate successfully predicts attribution errors, though weak-form score noise bias remains a primary limitation. Computed without knowledge of the truth, the D-optimal design selects test sets ranked second or third out of 126 candidates.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-constrained causal discovery can distinguish constitutive mechanisms from correlated environmental effects when trained on controlled interventions rather than observational data alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports constitutive models that generalize to unseen climates using full-field displacement measurements, without requiring measured stresses or internal variables.
method: Embed balance laws and constitutive skeletons in time-unrolled causal graphs scored by weak-form equilibrium gaps.
Use adaptive lasso and a NOTEARS-type acyclicity constraint to select mechanism dependencies and their evaluation order.
Use automatic differentiation to compute a local identifiability certificate and guide greedy D-optimal test design.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a synthetic plate study with 0.01-pixel displacement noise, interventional data recovered the exact 8-edge graph in 7 of 10 runs and kept unseen-climate errors within 3.2%, while strongly confounded observational data failed graph recovery and produced errors up to 41.5%.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is synthetic, and noise-induced bias in the weak-form score remains a primary limitation.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-constrained differentiable causal discovery of constitutive mechanisms through boundary value problems

title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear
authors: Sajjad Arzemanzadeh, Karol Miller, Ron Kikinis, Adam Wittek
abstract: The brain-skull interface governs the boundary/contact conditions of the brain in computational head models, yet its mechanical behaviour remains poorly characterised experimentally. We characterised the brain-skull interface by testing brain-skull complex samples (skull bone, meninges and brain tissue in their native arrangement) excised from 19 sheep cadaver heads under uniaxial tension and compression at strain rates of 0.002, 0.02 and 0.2 s$^{-1}$ and simple shear at 0.02 s$^{-1}$. Histology confirmed that the meningeal layers remained intact and attached to the brain and skull after excision. We acquired magnetic resonance images of every sample, reconstructed their geometry and developed a sample-specific finite element model of each experiment. We represented the brain tissue using a second-order Ogden hyperelastic model and the brain-skull interface using a cohesive zone model. Using inverse finite element analysis, we first calibrated the brain tissue parameters for each subject. Keeping these parameters fixed, we then identified the interface parameters from the corresponding brain-skull complex specimen. The brain tissue shear modulus increased with strain rate from 0.94 $\pm$ 0.16 kPa at 0.002 s$^{-1}$ to 1.60 $\pm$ 0.30 kPa at 0.2 s$^{-1}$. In contrast, the interface properties (maximum normal traction 2.35 $\pm$ 0.81 kPa, maximum tangential traction 4.14 $\pm$ 0.97 kPa, and fracture energy 0.35 $\pm$ 0.14 N m$^{-1}$) showed no significant dependence on strain rate or loading mode. In all samples, failure occurred within the subarachnoid space. Neither a rigid brain-skull connection nor frictionless sliding contact with separation reproduced the measured mechanical response or failure mode of the brain-skull interface. Our experimentally derived cohesive zone model provides a realistic representation of the brain-skull interface for computational head models.

infographic.key_insight: The intact brain–skull interface exhibits cohesive failure within the subarachnoid space, rather than behaving as a rigid connection or frictionless sliding contact.
infographic.engineering_relevance: An experimentally calibrated cohesive zone model offers more realistic brain–skull boundary conditions for computational head models.
method: Tested native brain–skull specimens from 19 sheep cadaver heads in tension, compression and shear.
Used histology to verify interface integrity and MRI to construct sample-specific finite element models.
Sequentially calibrated Ogden brain tissue and cohesive interface parameters using inverse finite element analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Interface properties showed no significant strain-rate or loading-mode dependence, with peak normal traction of 2.35 ± 0.81 kPa, peak tangential traction of 4.14 ± 0.97 kPa and fracture energy of 0.35 ± 0.14 N/m.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer to human head models and impact-rate loading requires validation beyond sheep cadaver specimens and the tested strain rates.
infographic.paper_title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear

title: Adapting a Vision Foundation Model for Fracture Characterization in Acoustic Image Logs
authors: Guangyu Wang, Xiaodong Ma, Xinming Wu
abstract: Natural fractures (NFs) and drilling-induced tensile fractures (DITFs) in acoustic image logs provide insights into rock mass structure and in situ stress, but manual characterization is time-consuming. Deep learning can automate this task, although expert-labeled data are scarce. We investigate whether adapting a pretrained vision foundation model (VFM) outperforms task-specific models trained from scratch with limited annotations. Using 80 annotated acoustic image samples, we fine-tuned DINOv3, pretrained on satellite imagery, and evaluated it on four boreholes excluded from fine-tuning. The adapted model estimated NF and DITF parameters comparably to human interpretation. Relative to U-Net, YOLOv8, and Swin Transformer models trained from scratch, it yielded fewer false positives and negatives and more accurate fracture counts and orientations. However, its performance advantage generally narrowed as training sample size decreased. We also assessed decoder architecture, fine-tuning strategy, and image enhancement. A progressive upsampling decoder with full fine-tuning performed best among the DINOv3 configurations tested, while fracture-focused image enhancement did not consistently improve accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of VFM adaptation for fracture characterization in acoustic image logs with limited labeled data and suggest a transferable workflow for other annotation-scarce geoscientific imaging tasks.

infographic.key_insight: Adapting pretrained DINOv3 improved fracture characterization in acoustic image logs over task-specific models trained from scratch with limited annotations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated characterization of natural and drilling-induced tensile fractures can support rock mass assessment and in situ stress interpretation while reducing manual effort.
method: Fine-tune satellite-imagery-pretrained DINOv3 on annotated acoustic image logs.
Compare against U-Net, YOLOv8, and Swin Transformer models trained from scratch.
Test decoder architecture, fine-tuning strategy, and fracture-focused image enhancement.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 80 annotated samples and evaluation on four held-out boreholes, adapted DINOv3 produced fracture parameter estimates comparable to human interpretation and fewer detection errors than the baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The performance advantage generally narrowed as training data decreased, and image enhancement did not consistently improve accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Adapting a Vision Foundation Model for Fracture Characterization in Acoustic Image Logs

title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
abstract: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

infographic.key_insight: Apparent advantages of real connectome wiring can reverse when model physiology is constrained by independent data rather than tuned for performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For computational model validation, structural comparisons need matched optimisation and independently constrained parameters to distinguish genuine structural effects from calibration bias.
method: Compare real-wiring physiology transferred to nulls (P1), separately tuned wiring models (P2), and data-constrained tuning (P3).
Test biological conclusions using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models.
Check robustness with held-out runs and extended retraining.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the mushroom-body model, real wiring beat a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but lost by 0.09 under P3; 95% confidence intervals excluded zero, and held-out runs confirmed the reversal.
infographic.watch_item: Failure under data-consistent physiology may reveal model inadequacy rather than inferior biological wiring; some flyvis rankings also depended on the retraining checkpoint.
infographic.paper_title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology

title: A pseudostress-based fully mixed finite element method for the stationary Biot--Poisson--Nernst--Planck system
abstract: We develop a pseudostress-based fully mixed finite element method for the stationary Biot-Poisson-Nernst-Planck system describing ionic transport in a charged, saturated, and deformable porous medium. The mechanical equations are reformulated in terms of a non-symmetric pseudostress and the solid displacement, while mixed formulations are retained for the Darcy, electrostatic, and ionic equations. The nonlinear electrostatic and advective couplings are treated in a Banach space setting. The formulation provides direct approximations of the pseudostress, fluxes, and concentration gradients, and permits algebraic reconstruction of the displacement gradient and Cauchy stress. Under block-stability and small-data assumptions, we establish continuous and discrete well-posedness, with poroelastic stability bounds uniform with respect to the first Lame parameter. A conforming Raviart-Thomas discretization, completed by discontinuous polynomials, yields a priori error estimates and convergence rates. For the coupled scheme in two dimensions, we construct a residual-based a posteriori error estimator and establish its reliability under an additional smallness condition on the prescribed data. Local efficiency is proved for polynomial boundary data, with boundary-data oscillation included for general traces. We also describe the estimator modifications for nonhomogeneous displacement and normal-flux data under corresponding stability and solvability hypotheses. Numerical experiments examine convergence of the mixed and reconstructed fields, robustness in the nearly incompressible regime, adaptive refinement, and ionic polarization in a charged porous medium.

infographic.key_insight: A pseudostress-based fully mixed finite element method couples porous-solid deformation, fluid flow, electrostatics, and ionic transport while retaining stability near incompressibility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports simulation of charged, fluid-saturated deformable porous media with direct access to stresses and transport fluxes.
method: Reformulate mechanics using non-symmetric pseudostress and displacement, with mixed Darcy, electrostatic, and ionic equations.
Discretize with conforming Raviart–Thomas elements and discontinuous polynomials; reconstruct displacement gradients and Cauchy stress algebraically.
Use a residual-based error estimator to guide adaptive refinement in two dimensions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports well-posedness and error estimates under stated assumptions, plus numerical studies of convergence, near-incompressible robustness, adaptivity, and ionic polarization.
infographic.watch_item: Well-posedness and estimator reliability require stability and small-data assumptions; the coupled estimator is established in two dimensions.
infographic.paper_title: A pseudostress-based fully mixed finite element method for the stationary Biot--Poisson--Nernst--Planck system

title: Partition of Unity Data-driven Finite Element Method for Anisotropic Diffusion in Magnetized Plasmas
abstract: Numerical simulation of transport processes in magnetized plasmas is characterized by extreme anisotropy, where diffusion along magnetic field lines can be many orders of magnitude larger than in the perpendicular direction. This anisotropy leads to thin, steep boundary layers and numerical pollution that standard finite element methods struggle to resolve without prohibitive mesh refinement. In this paper, we introduce the Partition of Unity Data-Driven Finite Element Method (PU-DDFEM), a data-driven local model reduction approach, for anisotropic diffusion. The method utilizes a bottom-up construction to enable a complete offline-online splitting. We parametrize the local magnetic field and boundary conditions to generate a snapshot space that captures the essential physics of plasma confinement. Dominant modes are extracted via a local spectral problem to identify representative features. These modes are then mapped to the global domain using a partition of unity to form a conforming approximation space. This ensures that the basis functions are fully reusable across different global magnetic configurations, significantly reducing the online computational overhead for large-scale plasma simulations.

infographic.key_insight: PU-DDFEM combines reusable, physics-informed local reduced bases into a conforming global space for strongly anisotropic diffusion in magnetized plasmas.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach aims to reduce the cost of plasma transport simulations where steep boundary layers otherwise demand extensive mesh refinement.
method: Generate local snapshots by parametrizing magnetic fields and boundary conditions.
Extract dominant local modes through a spectral problem.
Assemble modes using a partition of unity, enabling offline-online separation and reuse across global magnetic configurations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the method and its intended computational benefits but reports no quantitative accuracy, speedup, or benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy for unseen magnetic configurations may depend on how well local snapshot parameters cover the relevant field and boundary-condition variations.
infographic.paper_title: Partition of Unity Data-driven Finite Element Method for Anisotropic Diffusion in Magnetized Plasmas

title: Accelerating matrix-free fast diagonalization and preconditioned linear solvers for high-order finite element discretized elliptic problems on distributed GPUs
abstract: The time to solution of an iterative solver depends on the number of iterations and the cost per iteration. This paper develops algorithms that reduce both for elliptic problems discretized with high-order continuous finite elements on distributed GPUs, implemented in a unified matrix-free code supporting CUDA, HIP and SYCL. A distributed direct fast-diagonalization (FD) Poisson solver provides exact solutions on tensor-product meshes with direction-wise grading and coefficients varying along one coordinate direction. Its tensor data remain distributed, moved between slab layouts using collective transposes or kept in place by a Schur-complement approach. A two-level hybrid Schwarz preconditioner with FD cell solves (HS-FD) is extended to 2:1 hanging-node octrees with exact local cell inverses, while a p-multigrid preconditioner with Chebyshev--Jacobi smoothing (CJ-pMG) resolves hanging-node constraints at every level within fused kernels. Both approaches exploit FP32, where cell shapes and coefficients allow, within an FP64 conjugate-gradient iteration, adaptively select replicated or distributed coarse levels, support block solves for multiple right-hand sides and determine all parameters from the operator without case-specific tuning. Comparisons with Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients (Jacobi PCG), MFEM, nekRS and deal.II span uniform, graded and octree meshes, layered coefficients, and four applications across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs. The direct solver is two to three orders of magnitude faster than Jacobi PCG on uniform meshes. HS-FD converges in 11 iterations for the generalised Poisson problem on octree meshes across 8 to 1024 MI250X graphics compute dies. These results provide practical guidelines for solver selection based on mesh structure and coefficient characteristics.

infographic.key_insight: GPU-optimized matrix-free solvers accelerate high-order finite element elliptic problems by reducing both iteration counts and per-iteration costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster elliptic solves can reduce computational bottlenecks in large-scale finite element engineering simulations on distributed GPUs.
method: Distributed direct fast diagonalization for tensor-product meshes with direction-wise grading and coefficients varying along one coordinate.
FD-based hybrid Schwarz and Chebyshev–Jacobi p-multigrid preconditioners supporting hanging-node octrees.
Selective FP32 computation within FP64 conjugate gradients, adaptive coarse-level distribution and multiple-right-hand-side solves.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPU evaluations, the direct solver was 100–1,000× faster than Jacobi PCG on uniform meshes, while HS-FD converged in 11 iterations on tested octree problems across 8–1,024 MI250X graphics compute dies.
infographic.watch_item: Direct fast diagonalization requires compatible tensor-product structure and coefficients; solver choice and FP32 use depend on mesh and coefficient characteristics.
infographic.paper_title: Accelerating matrix-free fast diagonalization and preconditioned linear solvers for high-order finite element discretized elliptic problems on distributed GPUs

title: Design of Self-Folding Origami Architectures for Biomedical Implants: A Finite Element Simulation Framework
authors: Suhas Chandrashekar, Thomas Stieglitz, Prasanth Velvaluri
abstract: Minimally invasive brain implants require compact deployment geometries and controlled shape transformation for delivery through confined vessels. Origami-inspired structures enable large shape changes from compact to tailored deployed configurations, but implementation at microscale dimensions remains challenging, as conventional designs rely on predefined mountain and valley folds that become increasingly difficult to fabricate and assemble as unit-cell size is reduced to meet clinical requirements. To address this, we propose a self-folding methodology based on thermally induced stresses in thin-film bimetallic composites. Pairing the shape memory alloy Nitinol (NiTi) with molybdenum or stainless steel (SS316L) exploits their differing thermal expansion coefficients to generate localized hinge bending, enabling deterministic, autonomous folding into prescribed mountain and valley configurations. Using finite element simulations, we systematically optimize hinge length, layer thickness, width, and shape, identifying a hinge geometry achieving a ~50% reduction in unit-cell dimensions relative to previously reported designs. Integration into a complete waterbomb origami unit cell confirms that the strip-level folding mechanism scales to produce coordinated, self-folding deformation across the tessellated structure. These results demonstrate the feasibility of stress-induced, self-folding thin-film origami architectures built from clinically established biomaterials, providing a scalable design framework for next-generation, active neurovascular implants with integrated sensing and monitoring functionality.

infographic.key_insight: Finite element simulations show how thermally induced bending in NiTi-based bilayer hinges can drive coordinated self-folding of microscale origami for brain implants.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Self-folding thin-film structures could support compact delivery and controlled deployment of neurovascular implants in confined vessels.
method: Model thermal-stress-driven bending in NiTi–molybdenum and NiTi–SS316L bilayer hinges.
Optimize hinge length, layer thickness, width, and shape using finite element simulations.
Integrate hinges into a waterbomb origami unit cell to evaluate coordinated folding.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a simulated hinge design enabling approximately 50% smaller unit-cell dimensions than previously reported designs, plus coordinated self-folding in a complete waterbomb unit cell.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports simulation results, not experimental validation of microscale fabrication, deployment, or safe thermal actuation in vivo.
infographic.paper_title: Design of Self-Folding Origami Architectures for Biomedical Implants: A Finite Element Simulation Framework

title: Sparse, admissible and interpretable: discovery of isotropic limit surfaces with extended invariant libraries, physically gated mixtures of experts, and end-to-end structural identification
abstract: Choosing and fitting a limit surface, a yield or failure criterion, to multiaxial strength tests is a model-selection problem with physical side conditions. The equivalent stress concept provides a catalogue of criteria with admissibility conditions: convexity, a unique surface definition, explicit solvability, and bounds on inelastic Poisson ratios. We recast the task as sparse, constrained, differentiable model discovery and compare three representations. The first is a library of invariant monomials I1^a q^m r3^c containing classical criteria as sparse members. The second extends this library by trigonometric Lode-angle terms, restricted by isotropy to cosine modes, and Podgorski-Bigoni-Piccolroaz (PBP) atoms with learnable shape parameters. The third is a mixture of convex gauge experts using either a competition (smooth-maximum) or direction gate with hard-concrete and Gumbel-softmax sparsity. A ray-wise first-root definition gives explicit solvability and an exactly differentiable objective. Convexity and absence of re-entrant branches are differentiable penalties for the libraries and hold by construction for the competition gate. That gate acts as a physically motivated regime selector between mechanisms. Under stated assumptions its responsibilities are the share of failure probability in Weibull statistics, the share of dissipation in Koiter's multi-surface flow rule, and a Boltzmann weight in Gibbs principles. In synthetic benchmarks, the extended library recovers truths like Mohr-Coulomb and PBP surfaces within 1% error. We analyse five experimental datasets: two PMI foams, PA6, concrete, and TSSA in Hencky-strain space. A sharp Lode function matters more than many terms. With PBP atoms, concrete data are fitted with a fourfold lower error. End-to-end identification from notched-bar loads via differentiable finite elements removes nominal-stress mapping bias.

infographic.key_insight: Sparse, physics-constrained model discovery identifies interpretable isotropic yield and failure surfaces, with sharp Lode-angle dependence proving more valuable than many added terms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports multiaxial failure-model calibration while addressing physical admissibility and reducing nominal-stress mapping bias through differentiable finite-element identification.
method: Compare sparse invariant libraries, extensions with cosine Lode modes and learnable PBP atoms, and mixtures of convex gauge experts.
Use a differentiable ray-wise first-root objective with admissibility penalties; competition-gated mixtures preserve convexity by construction.
Identify model structure and parameters directly from notched-bar loads via differentiable finite elements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic Mohr–Coulomb and PBP surfaces are recovered within 1% error; five experimental datasets are analysed, with PBP atoms yielding fourfold lower fitting error for concrete.
infographic.watch_item: Library-based models rely on admissibility penalties rather than guarantees, so fitted surfaces require careful convexity and re-entrant-branch checks.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse, admissible and interpretable: discovery of isotropic limit surfaces with extended invariant libraries, physically gated mixtures of experts, and end-to-end structural identification

title: Soft material mechanical property degradation at high strain rates
authors: Victor Sanchez, Joseph Beckett, Aryan Shah, Sicong Wang, Jin Yang, Jonathan B. Estrada
abstract: The rheometry of soft, tissue-like materials at ultra-high strain rates is critical to biomechanics, materials science, and medical engineering. One approach for characterizing high-rate material response is Inertial Microcavitation Rheometry (IMR), which infers viscoelastic constitutive behavior from the measured radius-time history of a laser-induced cavitation bubble. At these rates, materials may exhibit history-dependent behavior, including damage, fracture, and plasticity. However, conventional IMR analyses typically assume constant material properties throughout the cavitation event, limiting their ability to capture such changes. We present an IMR framework for identifying effective time varying material properties from measured cavitation radius histories. The framework allows the shear modulus, viscosity, or both to evolve during the event using normalized sigmoid histories. Synthetic tests recover prescribed constant and time varying material histories. Application to polyacrylamide and gelatin datasets yields effective material-property histories across formulations and experimental conditions. Viscosity decreased across the datasets, while the extent of shear modulus reduction varied with material and formulation. When both properties decreased, their reductions could occur at different stages of cavitation. This distinction in mechanical property degradation depends on both the property and its evolution during high-strain events.

infographic.key_insight: High-rate cavitation can reveal effective viscosity and shear modulus reductions that occur at different stages, challenging constant-property assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tracking property changes during rapid deformation can improve characterization of soft, tissue-like materials for biomechanics and medical engineering.
method: Infer viscoelastic properties from laser-induced cavitation bubble radius–time histories using Inertial Microcavitation Rheometry.
Represent evolving shear modulus, viscosity, or both with normalized sigmoid histories.
Evaluate recovery on synthetic histories and apply the framework to polyacrylamide and gelatin datasets.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic tests recovered prescribed constant and evolving histories; experimental datasets showed viscosity decreases throughout, while shear modulus reductions varied by material and formulation.
infographic.watch_item: Inferred histories are effective properties constrained by sigmoid evolution and do not by themselves distinguish damage, fracture, and plasticity.
infographic.paper_title: Soft material mechanical property degradation at high strain rates

title: Analysis of TraceFEM for the Surface Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard Model
abstract: We analyze a trace finite element method (TraceFEM) for a surface fluid with a stabilization term that filters out Killing vector fields, and use it to discretize the surface Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard problem in space only. Assuming no geometric error, we show that the discrete inf-sup condition that our method requires is equivalent to the usual condition found in the literature and known to hold for trace Taylor-Hood pairs of arbitrary order in intrinsic dimension two. Inspired by a continuous dependence estimate at the PDE level, we derive error estimates for our scheme in the energy norms, which in turn lead to estimates in $L^2$-norms and, for two-dimensional surfaces, $L^\infty$-norm for the phase variable. To that end, we introduce a $p$-dependent scaling for the normal derivative volume stabilization, and use it to prove new approximation and inverse estimates in the $L^p$- and $W^{1,p}$-based setting ($p \in [1,\infty]$ for approximation and $p \in [2,\infty]$ for inverse estimates). Finally, we corroborate the analysis with numerical experiments.

infographic.key_insight: TraceFEM provides provable error control for the spatial discretization of coupled surface Stokes–Cahn–Hilliard flow, assuming no geometric error.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The analysis supports reliable finite element simulation of coupled fluid flow and phase separation on surfaces.
method: Use TraceFEM with stabilization that filters out Killing vector fields.
Establish discrete inf-sup equivalence for trace Taylor–Hood pairs.
Introduce p-dependent normal-derivative stabilization to derive approximation, inverse, and solution-error estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports energy- and L²-norm error estimates, phase-variable L∞ estimates on two-dimensional surfaces, and corroborating numerical experiments.
infographic.watch_item: The analysis assumes exact geometry and discretizes space only, so geometric approximation and time-integration errors require separate assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Analysis of TraceFEM for the Surface Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard Model

title: The norm, not the labels: training and evaluating finite-element surrogates for stress analysis in the energy norm
abstract: Finite-element surrogates predict the stresses of a new design in one evaluation, but are usually trained on solutions with a displacement loss and compared by it, although engineering decisions rest on stresses. Application in engineering: stress analysis of perforated plates and solids with cavities, parametric families in which holes concentrate stress. Contribution to artificial intelligence: training and evaluating such surrogates in the energy norm, with or without solutions, and screening their predictions without solutions. For linear elastostatics, minimising the assembled discrete potential energy is exactly supervised regression in this norm: the energy gap of a prediction is the strain energy of its stress error. A displacement loss under-weights the stiff modes that carry the strains. In pre-registered comparisons, changing only the norm of the supervised loss cut a three-dimensional transformer's median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and its median von Mises error 6.1-fold; in two dimensions it more than halved the von Mises error, also on held-out instances. In three dimensions, the transformer trained on the energy alone came within a factor of 1.3 of the energy-norm-supervised one in median energy-norm and von Mises error. It was more accurate than the displacement-supervised one on all five metrics in every seed. Given the stiffness matrix, a Ritz projection was more accurate than the label-free transformer, in the seed means, on every metric but peak stress. No network transferred to a substantially finer mesh. The energy ranks predictions of a load case, and its sign flags those worse than the zero field.

infographic.key_insight: For linear elastostatics, training finite-element surrogates in the energy norm targets stress accuracy, and minimizing discrete potential energy is exactly equivalent to supervised regression in that norm.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Energy-based training supports stress prediction in perforated plates and solids with cavities, where stress concentrations drive engineering decisions.
method: Replace displacement loss with energy-norm supervision.
Train without solution labels by minimizing assembled discrete potential energy.
Screen predictions without solutions: energy ranks candidates for a load case, and its sign flags predictions worse than the zero field.
infographic.evidence_signal: In pre-registered comparisons, changing only the supervised loss norm reduced a 3D transformer's median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and median von Mises error 6.1-fold; in 2D, von Mises error more than halved, including on held-out instances.
infographic.watch_item: No network transferred to a substantially finer mesh, limiting claims of mesh generalization.
infographic.paper_title: The norm, not the labels: training and evaluating finite-element surrogates for stress analysis in the energy norm

title: F3-AGI v4.0: Bioenergetically-Gated Active Inference, Metaplastic Preconditioning, and Residual Program Synthesis for Sample-Efficient Abstract Reasoning
abstract: Few-shot abstract reasoning on ARC-AGI requires inducing algorithmic transformations from 2 to 5 demonstration pairs without task-specific pretraining. Because few-shot demonstrations under-constrain the hypothesis space, program synthesis suffers from the Rashomon effect (predictive multiplicity): heuristic search finds spurious programs with low training error that fail on test inputs, while unconstrained library growth degrades latency. We introduce F3-AGI v4.0, a CPU-native neuro-symbolic and active inference architecture comprising three mechanisms: (1) F3-Metabolic-Optim, combining mistake-gated plasticity, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, and virtual ATP gating; (2) Adaptive Complexity-Guided Program Synthesis (AACR) with a Cycle-3 ResidualPatchSynthesizer and smallest-pair early rejection; and (3) a 512D L2-normalized random projection driving Expected Free Energy (EFE) exploration with dead-signature pruning. Across three empirical studies: (i) on a synthetic 5-task class-incremental stream without replay, F3-Metabolic-Optim achieves 91.67% final accuracy with 9.17% forgetting, skipping 93.47% of updates, cutting L1 plasticity cost by 65.7%, and running 2.19x faster than EWC; (ii) on the 400-task ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set (offline CPU, zero LLM calls), F3-AGI v4.0 solves 57/400 tasks (14.25% pass@2; 56/400 pass@1) with a mean latency of 1.62 s/task, decomposed into 19/50 (38.00%, 1.19 s/task, a 42.5x paired speedup over Horizon 2) on the 50-task calibration slice and 38/350 (10.86%) on the 350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks (with 7 autonomous Cycle-3 patch solutions); and (iii) in a local 5-game (15-level) ARC-AGI-3-inspired interactive suite, our agent completes 15/15 levels with 89.44% level-weighted RHAE (90.72% unweighted).

infographic.key_insight: F3-AGI v4.0 combines gated learning, complexity-guided program synthesis, and active exploration for CPU-native, few-shot abstract reasoning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its resource-aware learning and symbolic search may inform efficient engineering AI, but the abstract provides no solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling validation.
method: Gate plasticity using mistakes, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, and a virtual ATP budget.
Search programs with complexity guidance, residual patch synthesis, and smallest-pair early rejection.
Guide Expected Free Energy exploration with 512D random projections and dead-signature pruning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported results include 57/400 ARC-AGI-1 tasks solved at pass@2 with 1.62 s/task mean latency, 91.67% final accuracy on a synthetic continual-learning stream, and 15/15 levels completed in a local interactive suite.
infographic.watch_item: ARC performance was lower on strictly uninspected hold-out tasks (10.86%) than on the calibration slice (38.00%), highlighting generalization limits.
infographic.paper_title: F3-AGI v4.0: Bioenergetically-Gated Active Inference, Metaplastic Preconditioning, and Residual Program Synthesis for Sample-Efficient Abstract Reasoning
